title: AI capability depends on local complements and can expand capacity while deepening concentration risk
source_unit: World Bank World Development Report 2026 framework and chapter-level synthesis; developing-country perspective with US-relevant value-chain implications
geography: Global/developing-country analytical frame; US is a value-chain and institutional comparison case, not the report's sole population

required_complements.value: infrastructure, skills, institutions, data, and local-language fit

observations.method: World Bank flagship report synthesis of research, country evidence, and policy analysis; framework is interpretive and strategic rather than a single statistical estimator.
observations.uncertainty: The framework does not provide one comparable effect size or a US population estimate. Recommendations and chapter conclusions must remain distinct from measured country or firm outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Developing economies, firms, governments, and people facing different infrastructure, skill, institutional, and language conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Imported tools can deliver useful capability without local frontier-model production; local adaptation is not automatically cheaper, safer, or more effective.

observations.period: 2026; AI diffusion and capability concentration claims

denominator.unit: World Bank report comparative technology-diffusion frame

middle_income_share_global_chatgpt_traff.unit: percent of global ChatGPT traffic, report-described comparison

observations.method: World Bank report comparison of technology diffusion timelines and ChatGPT traffic evidence.
observations.uncertainty: These are report-level comparative claims with different technologies, definitions, and denominators; they do not establish equal access, productive use, or welfare gains.
observations.subgroup: Lower-income and middle-income countries compared across technologies.
observations.counterinterpretation: Fast traffic or tool diffusion can reflect experimentation and access without local institutional fit, reliable infrastructure, or durable productive adoption.

observations.period: 2026; AI value-chain concentration and dependency analysis

concentrated_layers.value: hardware, infrastructure, models, and applications are concentrated in a few countries and companies

frontier_building_requirement.value: chips, large data centers, data, and specialized researchers

observations.method: World Bank value-chain and political-economy synthesis.
observations.uncertainty: The report's concentration statement is not a US supplier Herfindahl estimate or a country-specific switching-cost calculation.
observations.subgroup: Countries, governments, firms, and individuals positioned differently across the AI value chain.
observations.counterinterpretation: Concentration can lower entry costs by allowing countries to adopt and customize existing tools; dependency risk and access benefit can coexist.

denominator.unit: World Bank report policy and chapter synthesis

public_service_examples.value: weather forecasting, health screening, agriculture extension, education, tax enforcement, and administration

front_end_evaluation_gap.value: limited evidence for selecting, procuring, and evaluating front-end public-service AI

observations.method: World Bank synthesis of reported AI use and public-sector capability requirements.
observations.uncertainty: Examples and institutional gaps are not a prevalence estimate, impact evaluation, or proof that AI improved service recipients' outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Public agencies, service workers, and residents using health, education, agricultural, tax, and legal services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Back-end or pilot use may improve administrative capacity without producing accessible or trusted front-end service; procurement and evaluation can change that result.

denominator.unit: World Bank chapter 6 and governance synthesis

identified_risks.value: dependency, capital concentration, surveillance, propaganda, public-budget pressure, and regulatory-capacity gaps

observations.method: World Bank political and institutional analysis of AI value chains, public capacity, and governance.
observations.uncertainty: The chapter identifies mechanisms and policy questions; it does not observe a specific change in US leverage, alliance behavior, public legitimacy, or citizen trust.
observations.subgroup: States, firms, public agencies, and individuals with unequal control over models, chips, data centers, data, and enforcement.
observations.counterinterpretation: Government procurement, international cooperation, open standards, and local adaptation may reduce dependence; the report does not measure which intervention succeeds in a given place.

related_sources.claim: World Bank provides a reproducibility package with chapter-specific data, code, dependencies, and verified reproduction notes.
related_sources.access_boundary: The package includes a mix of data, code, proprietary inputs, and chapter outputs; not every source is locally available.

related_sources.claim: World Bank's data-infrastructure results brief supplies project-level context for digital complements and country cases.
Registered World Bank Open Data landing page for separating report frameworks from country indicator data.

boundary: This is a World Bank framework and report-evidence record, not a US AI adoption, productivity, or geopolitical-leverage estimate. It contributes a capability/dependency mechanism and identifies measurable complements, concentration, public procurement, and governance stages. Country, firm, household, and state effects require separate primary records and compatible denominators.
